name: Karl Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel, and this conversation is confidential. What is an ordinary shift building or repairing power lines like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an electricity company crew, so the first thing is checking our permits and who does each isolation. I have a two-year technical diploma, but after years on the lines I can usually tell from the sound of a transformer when a ticket has missed something.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what makes the shift harder at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like coaching the newer hands through a fault without making them feel foolish. My partner Leila and I have two children at school and a mortgage; my lead pay is low for the work, and we have less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a little AI help with routine reports is fine if we still check every isolation ourselves. I use a tool now and then to shorten a long fault note, but I never copy its numbers into a permit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the quiet scenario is a relief for the job, but not for our finances. A flat pay packet leaves almost nothing after the mortgage and children’s costs, and few nearby firms hire lineworkers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading repairs and comparing every report with our signed permit. I’d cancel the monthly streaming package this week and use the saved fee for the electricity bill in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household money, even if AI stays modest. It would be nice to spend less of a Sunday counting bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which number would you never copy from the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the switch identifier from the signed permit and read it back to a crew member. A fluent paragraph cannot tell me the line is dead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the cancelled package actually save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is about twenty a month, which sounds small until a bill is short by twenty. Leila and I can borrow films from the local library instead.

say: **Routine reports** may get quicker, but the crew checks each isolation.
I sometimes shorten **fault notes** with AI and verify every number before use.
think: Our **thin savings** make flat pay stressful despite little change to linework.
Few **local jobs** mean I value the existing crew post.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and checking reports against signed permits.
**Cancel** the monthly streaming package and use its twenty for the electricity bill.
feel: **Anxious** about present bills, while the job itself looks steady.
S0.quote: A fluent paragraph cannot tell me the line is dead.
fieldNote: Karl uses **AI occasionally** for wording, while keeping permit numbers under crew control.
The cancelled **monthly fee** is small, yet the bill it covers shows how little spare cash remains.

steps.text: Keep checking fault reports against signed permits
Cancel the monthly streaming package for the electricity bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew AI will probably change dispatch orders and parts lists first, not the hands that replace a failed insulator. I would try the new ticket screen after another crew has tested it and shown where its errors appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a quicker office could load more calls onto our truck without lifting my pay. A robot may come later, but the immediate risk is a tired crew trying to meet a neat timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a neighbouring crew lead to show me their trial ticket and its error log. During the first year I’d learn the screen if its checks are clear, then compare its parts list with what we find at each pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the pressure on the crew and anxious about our tight budget. A tired crew cannot be repaired by a neat timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error would change your view of the screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the list repeatedly left out the connector we need, I would want a human sign-off before it reached the truck. One bad list is a fixable problem; repeated bad lists are a process problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for more pay if call volume rose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring our call records to my manager and ask for the lead rate to be reviewed. I would not count a raise until it appears in a pay packet.

say: **Dispatch tickets** and parts lists change before much physical linework does.
I would try the **new screen** after another crew has tested its errors.
think: More **calls** could arrive without more pay for my lead responsibilities.
The immediate concern is a **tired crew** working to a software timetable.
do: **Review** a neighbouring crew’s trial ticket and error log.
**Learn** the ticket screen if its checks are clear, then compare listed parts with poles.
**Request** a lead pay review if call volume rises.
feel: **Anxious** about a thin household cushion and extra crew pressure.
S1.quote: A tired crew cannot be repaired by a neat timetable.
fieldNote: He is **steady** rather than first in line: another crew must test the screen before he adopts it.
His **pay request** depends on actual call growth and is not treated as a guaranteed raise.

steps.text: Review another crew’s trial ticket and error log
Learn the ticket screen if its checks prove clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI by 2028 could run the office, while crews still handle the line until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would ask who has authority to stop a robot job when a pole is weaker than the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our company may need fewer crews once robots can work on lines, and I cannot bridge a lost wage with less than a month saved. My technical diploma helps, but there are few other lineworker posts close to our children’s school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the manager for the planned crew numbers and stop-work rule before the first robot trial. I’d stop our paid weekend outings now, and I’d check whether the regional utility has any field inspection vacancy rather than assume one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, even though I can learn a machine once it is proven. A short timetable leaves the mortgage no room for a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the outings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them we are choosing free walks and games for a while because the family budget is tight. I would not promise the paid outings will return by a date I cannot know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if there is an inspection vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d read its pay and travel conditions before applying, because a longer drive could cancel the gain. If it offered enough to cover the mortgage and school routine, I would apply.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes dispatch before robots reach line repair around 2031.
I would ask for a **stop-work rule** before a robot trial.
think: Fewer **crew jobs** could leave our mortgage uncovered with under a month saved.
A technical **diploma** helps, but few nearby lineworker posts fit the children’s school routine.
do: **Ask** the manager for planned crew numbers and stop-work authority.
**Stop** paid weekend outings and choose free family activities.
**Check** regional inspection vacancies, applying only if pay and travel work.
feel: **Alarmed** about a likely lost wage and a short runway.
S2.quote: A short timetable leaves the mortgage no room for a mistake.
fieldNote: He is willing to use a **proven machine**, but the calendar and savings make the household vulnerable.
His alternative **vacancy** is conditional on an opening and workable pay and travel, not an assured move.

steps.text: Stop paid weekend outings for free family activities
Check regional inspection vacancies and apply if pay and travel work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AI by 2031 and robots around 2034 leave time to run tests on dead lines and train crews. I would watch a proven field trial before asking my own crew to use the equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I could see myself moving into inspection, but I need a post that pays at least what I earn now. With our thin reserve, I cannot take unpaid training and hope a vacancy appears later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our training lead this year for the field-trial schedule and any paid inspection course linked to a vacancy. If the company offers paid time and a suitable post, I’d take the course; until then I’d keep leading repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives us time to check each promise. A course has to lead somewhere my family can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see at the field trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want to see the robot stop when the plan misses a cracked crossarm and hand the decision back to the crew. I would also ask how a worker records that refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as suitable pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job would need to cover our mortgage and the extra travel after tax. I cannot name a precise figure until I see a real offer and its hours.

say: **2031 thinking AI** comes before capable line robots around 2034.
I would watch a **field trial** before our crew uses new equipment.
think: An **inspection role** interests me only if its pay covers mortgage and travel.
Unpaid **training** is too risky with less than a month saved.
do: **Request** the field-trial schedule and any paid inspection course tied to a vacancy.
**Take** the course only if paid time and a suitable post are offered.
**Continue** leading line repairs while those conditions remain unmet.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough time to verify the job and course terms.
S3.quote: A course has to lead somewhere my family can afford.
fieldNote: His potential **course** has two explicit conditions: paid time and a post with workable income.
He wants the robot to **hand back control** at a cracked crossarm, a field test tied to his craft.

steps.text: Request the field-trial schedule and paid course terms
Take a paid inspection course if a suitable post is offered
Continue leading repairs until course and job terms are met

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 give us a decade to write sensible inspection rules. We can compare machines with experienced crews through several seasons, not one show day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be in my fifties by the robot date, so less climbing could suit me. Yet I need paid work through the mortgage years, and I would not sell our house or retire early on an idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next year I’d write down the faults our crew catches that a ticket missed and show the list at the annual safety review. I’d keep using AI occasionally for fault-note wording, and take a proven inspection module later only if the company pays and offers a role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the long change and anxious about the same bills we have today. A decade lets me make a careful choice if our wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which faults belong on the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start with water damage inside an apparently sound junction box and a loose connection hidden behind a cover. Photos and the crew’s test results would sit beside each note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave your crew before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave for a real inspection post with secure hours and enough net pay for the mortgage. I would not leave for a promise of work after a training course.

say: **2036 thinking AI** and robots around 2039 leave years for seasonal line trials.
I would use **crew faults** to shape inspection rules.
think: Less **climbing** could suit me later, but the mortgage still needs paid work.
I would not **retire early** or move house on an unproven job idea.
do: **Document** hidden line faults for the next annual safety review.
**Continue** occasional checked AI wording in fault notes.
**Consider** a paid inspection module only with a suitable company role.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills, though longer timing eases the career decision.
S4.quote: I would not leave for a promise of work after a training course.
fieldNote: The **long runway** allows seasons of comparison and a gradual move toward inspection if paid work exists.
His **retirement** comment is a refusal, not an action; the mortgage remains a firm constraint.

steps.text: Document hidden line faults for the annual safety review
Continue checking occasional AI wording in fault notes
Consider paid inspection training only with a suitable role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a crew cut after the robots arrive could take our mortgage money before we have built a reserve. I need a clear stop-work rule, honest crew numbers and paid training linked to a real job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the new inspection posts will still let a parent get home when school closes. A higher wage is not much help if the commute swallows the children’s afternoons.

headlineQuote: A higher wage is not much help if the commute swallows the children’s afternoons.
portrait: Karl is an experienced **line crew lead** with a technical diploma, two schoolchildren, a mortgage and under a month saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for wording and adopts new systems after another crew proves their checks.
Lower **lead pay** and scarce nearby jobs keep his household anxious even in the mild scenario.
He would consider **paid inspection training** if a real post covers the mortgage and travel.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink crews after robots arrive before he builds a mortgage reserve.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **stop-work rule**, honest crew numbers and paid training tied to an actual job would help.
